In `cmd.exe`, its value is a string of PowerShell code; Microsoft says it must be the final PowerShell parameter, with following text treated as part of the command. So when a batch file appends `%*`, PowerShell parses that text as code—not as a preserved list of original arguments. Quotes around a value with spaces may keep it together, but only if they survive `cmd.exe`’s parsing and remain meaningful in the PowerShell command. ([learn.microsoft.com](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/powershell/module/microsoft.powershell.core/about/about_powershell_exe?view=powershell-5.1))

**Prefer `-File` for forwarding arguments to a script:**

```bat
@echo off
powershell.exe -NoProfile -File "%~dp0target.ps1" %*
```

The script path is quoted for spaces; callers should quote each argument containing spaces, for example:

```bat
wrapper.bat "two words" "C:\path with spaces\file.txt"
```

`-File` passes subsequent values as script parameters, after the calling shell has interpreted them. That is more appropriate than embedding forwarded values in PowerShell source, though `cmd.exe` still has its own quoting and special-character rules. In **Windows PowerShell 5.1**, `cmd.exe` and PowerShell parse the text in separate stages:

1. In a batch file, `%*` expands to the batch arguments. It is not a structured argument array; it’s text inserted into the command line. ([learn.microsoft.com](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/previous-versions/windows/it-pro/windows-server-2012-r2-and-2012/cc732835%28v%3Dws.11%29))
2. `cmd.exe` processes that command line first. Quotes can group text with spaces, but characters such as `&`, `|`, and parentheses have `cmd` meanings and may need escaping or quoting. ([learn.microsoft.com](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows-server/administration/windows-commands/cmd))
3. `powershell.exe -Command` treats the remaining input as **PowerShell code**. From `cmd.exe`, it does not receive a PowerShell script-block object; it receives a string to parse as code. ([learn.microsoft.com](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/powershell/module/microsoft.powershell.core/about/about_powershell_exe?view=powershell-5.1))

So a wrapper like:

```bat
powershell.exe -NoProfile -Command "%*"
```

does **not** safely forward arbitrary caller arguments as data. For example, quotes or metacharacters in an argument can be interpreted or altered by `cmd.exe` and then PowerShell, and an argument containing spaces may not retain the boundaries you intended.

**If you want to run a script and pass arguments, prefer `-File`:**

```bat
powershell.exe -NoProfile -File "%~dp0script.ps1" %*
```

The script path is quoted; `%*` expands the caller’s arguments.
